title: Nzema: Kings, a Village on Water, and a Philosopher

pages.text: From the village of Beyin, a canoe takes you inland along a narrow channel through reeds and raffia palms. After nearly an hour, the channel opens into a wide, dark lake. Ahead, a whole village stands on the water. Houses, a school, a church, and a single main street all rest on wooden stilts. Children paddle to class. This is Nzulezo, whose name means on the surface of the water. It is one of the wonders of Nzemaland, the home of the Nzema people in the south-western corner of Ghana.

pages.text: How did a village come to be built on a lake? Tradition says that the ancestors of Nzulezo fled from enemies in a land far to the north. They were guided by a snail, which led them from place to place until they reached this lake, where no attacker could come near without being seen. The rest of the Nzema lived along the coast and beside the lagoons. They fished and farmed coconuts and oil palms. They also traded with European ships. In the 1700s, the British built a small fort at Beyin and named it Apollonia.

pages.text: The Nzema kingdom reached its height in the 1830s and 1840s under a king named Kaku Aka. He was a strong and feared ruler who controlled trade along his coast and would not take orders from the British at Cape Coast. The British accused him of cruelty and of breaking agreements. In 1848, they sent an armed force against him. Kaku Aka was captured and taken to Cape Coast Castle, where he died a prisoner. After his fall, the kingdom was divided into eastern and western Nzema, each with its own chiefs.

pages.text: Each year, the Nzema and their Ahanta neighbours celebrate the Kundum festival. It moves along the coast from town to town over several weeks. Tradition says that a hunter once saw forest spirits dancing in a circle and brought the dance home. Kundum gives thanks for the harvest and drives out evil from the town. For some days, people may sing songs that mock those who have done wrong, including chiefs. Drummers play through the night, and families who have quarrelled are expected to make peace before the feast. It is a time of joy and of judgement.

pages.text: Nzemaland has given the world two remarkable men. Around 1703, a boy was born near Axim and taken to Europe as a small child. He was given the name Anton Wilhelm Amo. He studied law and philosophy, and he became a lecturer at universities in Germany. He was the first African known to have done so. He later returned home. Two centuries after him, in 1909, a boy was born at Nkroful to a goldsmith and a trader. His name was Kwame Nkrumah. In 1957, he led the Gold Coast to independence as Ghana.

pages.text: Today the fort at Beyin is a museum of Nzema history, and the wetland around Nzulezo is protected for its birds, monkeys, and turtles. Visitors pay to see the village, and the money helps the community. Oil and gas are now produced off the Nzema coast, which brings both jobs and new worries for fishermen. The Nzema story is a reminder that a small people in a far corner of the country can shape the whole nation. It is also a reminder to look after the places that make such a people who they are.
